title: Vayera: shall not the judge do justly? (Genesis 18:25)
hookLine: Abraham asks "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?"

cards: Pushing back on someone with far more power is its own hard skill. A boss. A judge.
A doctor. A parent, years ago. Every word gets chosen carefully: with respect, I don't think that's fair.
In this portion, someone says that to God. Three visitors have eaten at Abraham's tent and are heading toward Sodom, and God decides to tell Abraham what's about to happen to that city.
What Abraham says next is a question about God's own justice.

teach.b: First, the text lets you hear God weighing it: shall I hide from Abraham what I am doing? God decides not to, because Abraham is meant to teach his children to do righteousness and justice.
So God says: the outcry from Sodom is great, and its sin is very grievous. And Abraham steps forward. Would you destroy the righteous with the wicked?
What if there are fifty righteous people in the city? That be far from you. And then the line: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?"
Think about who he's saying it to. God agrees: for fifty, I'll spare the whole place. Then Abraham keeps going.
I, "who am but dust and ashes," what if there are forty-five? Forty? Thirty?
Twenty? Ten? Each time, God says yes.
Abraham stops at ten, and the story leaves it there. Notice three things. First, Abraham is arguing for strangers.
Sodom isn't his city; its king is the one whose wealth he refused. He argues for them anyway.

teach.h: DUST AND ASHES, AND STILL ASKING.
teach.b: Second, he's humble and bold at once: dust and ashes, and still asking.
Some readers go further: God shared the plan because Abraham is meant to teach justice, so speaking up is the point.
Later Jewish voices pick up the thread: Moses pleading for his people, Jeremiah and Job asking why, and in Hasidic stories, a rebbe who calls God to a trial on behalf of his people.
In this story, the man chosen to teach justice is the one who asks God for it.

how: Jewish teachers often point to Abraham's plea for Sodom as the model for arguing with God on behalf of justice, a thread that runs through the prophets, the Psalms and Hasidic stories.

o: and he built, Abraham's altar at Hebron
and he appeared, the portion's first word
and he argued, Abraham's plea for Sodom

s: God rebukes Abraham for questioning him
God answers each time, and never rebukes him.
Abraham argues for his own city
Sodom isn't his; he argues for strangers.
fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten.

games.q: you're Abraham. God has just told you Sodom may be destroyed. what do you do?
o: ask: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?
warn Lot and leave the rest.
games.why: Abraham argues, humbly and boldly, for fifty, then down to ten. God says yes each time.

practice: Think of a group you're tempted to write off completely: a city, a crowd, the other side of an argument.
Then ask Abraham's question, fifty good people there, or forty, or ten, and picture even one of them going about an ordinary day until they're real to you.

wordCard.voice: Vayera. The portion where God appears to Abraham, and Abraham argues for a city of strangers: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?

orig.note: Hebrew: and he appeared; the first word of the portion.

carryVoice: Your line: justice, even from God. Dust and ashes, and still asking. Day one hundred seventy-seven in the books.
